display.title: Confessed, Not Said: Precision in the Kinnim Viduy

learning.ahaMoment: Precision matters: 'after he confessed' captures the act of atonement through words, while 'after he said' is merely descriptive.
learning.memoryAnchor: 'Confessed' vs 'said' - the former is the halachic category; the Gemara insists on precision in describing the atoning act.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does the Gemara insist on saying 'after he confessed' rather than 'after he said,' and what closes out the kinnim discussion?
learning.coreTension: Describing the High Priest's first confession only as 'he said' would describe mere speech, but the formula needs to capture viduy as a halachic act of confession, not just an utterance.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara corrects the language to 'after he confessed' (hitvadeh), establishing that the formula must name the legal category of confession itself, not merely report that words were spoken.

takeaway.text: The formula must say 'after he confessed,' not 'after he said' - confession (viduy) is the legal category that carries atonement, and the Gemara insists the language used to describe it conveys that category precisely.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may treat 'said' and 'confessed' as interchangeable since both describe speech, missing that only 'confessed' names the halachic act of viduy that carries atonement.

display.title: The Azazel Goat's Organized Journey: Ten Booths to the Tsuk

learning.ahaMoment: The Azazel goat's journey was organized and companioned - not abandoned. The infrastructure of booths reflects the community's active participation in the ceremony.
learning.memoryAnchor: 10 booths = 10 stations = organized ritual journey for the goat, with national support along the way.
learning.learnerQuestion: How was the Azazel goat actually sent to the wilderness, and was it truly abandoned alone?
learning.coreTension: The Torah commands the goat be sent away by the hand of a designated man, but the Mishna's description of ten staffed booths and an accompanying retinue raises the question of how much communal structure surrounded what could be read as a solitary act of abandonment.
learning.coreMove: The Mishna details ten booths from Jerusalem to the Tsuk, each offering the ish iti food and drink and a relay of escorts to the next station, showing the sending was a structured, accompanied journey rather than the goat being left alone from the start.

takeaway.text: The Azazel goat's journey to the Tsuk was an organized, staffed, and escorted procession of ten booths spanning 12 mil, not a solitary abandonment - communal structure surrounded the sending even as the goat itself was finally left alone at the cliff.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may picture the goat as simply turned loose into the wilderness alone, missing the elaborate infrastructure of ten booths, provisions, and escorts that organized its journey.

rashiTranslations.en: Rashi: opens - what question arises? And [the problem is that] here [in the Mishna's language] it is neither the time of taking nor the time of performance.
Rashi: continues - and [the Gemara] fixes it: do not say 'and afterward [the High Priest] said' but rather 'and afterward [he] took [the goat] and said.'
Rashi: continues - [this is] for the chatat and this [is] for the olah - [they were] performing Tannaim's teaching [with] a deficiency of one word through forgetfulness.
Rashi: continues - and it was confused for them between 'and afterward [he] took' and '[and afterward he] said' - and we raise difficulty.
Rashi: continues - [he] took [the goat] - if so he added and brought his obligation [of the chatat].
Rashi: continues - from an animal [purchased] from the money [designated for] his chatat - what is it? Behold
Rashi: continues - it is not money, since [he] already took the bird [for his offering].
Rashi: continues - he redeems it - and takes it out to the profane [use] and adds [money from] his house.
Rashi: continues - and purchases from the money an animal [for the offering].
Rashi: continues - and [yet there is] a difficulty: there is no redemption for birds - because so we learn [it].
Rashi: continues - in Tractate Menachot (folio 100:) [that] regarding birds, frankincense, and the priestly vessel there is no redemption.
Rashi: continues - for it was not said except regarding an animal [alone].
Rashi: continues - such as [he] took one young pigeon - a single [pigeon], he took from the [community] treasury money.
Rashi: continues - and thus said [the] Tanna [of the Mishna].
Rashi: continues - if [it was designated for] an olah, [he] sold - this money that stood for a chatat [are now] becoming chatat and he added on them and brought his obligation.
Rashi: continues - and this olah that he sold went to a voluntary [offering].

Rashi: continues - if [it was designated for] a chatat [he] sold - the community money were established for an olah through this taking, and [he] does not add on them and bring his obligation from them.
Rashi: opens [new Mishna section] - but [rather] he brings from the money [designated for an] olah [as a] voluntary offering, and the chatat that he took dies.
Rashi: continues - and from his house he will bring money and will take [an animal].
Rashi: continues - but [it is] different regarding the metzora - it is written [in Scripture]: 'This is the law of the metzora.'
Rashi: continues - and not another [law applies].

Rashi: continues - [and regarding] the first part [of the Mishna] also - the head of it [i.e., the ruling]: there is one Torah for all the metzora'im - they all go out [satisfying their obligation] with the offering of a rich [man].
Rashi: continues - and the teaching is [also found] [with reference to a source].
Rashi: continues - and [from] it we derive: [one who becomes] impure desecrates the Holy [foods].
Rashi: continues - and if [he is] poor, [the defilement is limited] - it is a limitation [in the scope of who becomes] impure.
Rashi: continues - [the one who is] impure [who brings the] offering of a poor man does not fulfill [his obligation].
Rashi: continues - but other [those] obligated for [ascending and descending] offering do not [fulfill through] ascending and descending [poverty offerings].
Rashi: continues - [The Mishna states:] [He tied the scarlet thread] opposite [its] place of sending-out - opposite the gate through which they took it out.
Rashi: continues - and for slaughter [is stated also] - [this] will be explained in the Gemara.
Rashi: opens [Gemara discussion] - [the Gemara asks:] Is it a binding that it stands? Or [is it] an erecting that it stands?
Rashi: continues - [i.e., does the rule requiring separation apply to] the binding [of the thread] to the head of the Azazel goat, or to the erecting of the goat opposite its place?
Rashi: continues - Come [and hear from the teaching]: For so R. Yosef taught: He tied a scarlet thread to the head of the Azazel goat.
Rashi: continues - and [he] erect[ed] it opposite [its] place of sending-out, and the goat for slaughter [is erected] opposite [its] place of slaughter.
Rashi: continues - so that they not be mixed one with another and not be mixed with others.

Rashi: continues - [But] if you concede that [it is] an erecting that it stands - [although] indeed they are not mixed one with another, [since] this one burns [the offering] with it and this one does not burn with it,
Rashi: continues - [nevertheless] with others [goats] it would be mixed.
Rashi: continues - [Therefore] rather [it is] not an erecting that it stands, [but rather] a binding that it stands.
Rashi: continues - Hear [from this]: R. Yitzchak [said]: Two scarlet threads I heard.
Rashi: continues - One of the [red] heifer, and one of the Azazel goat - one needs [a] measure [of a certain weight].
Rashi: continues - and one does not need [a] measure - and we do not know which [is] which.
Rashi: continues - [R. Yosef] said: Let us see - [the thread] of the Azazel goat [since it] requires a division [of half on the rock, half on the goat] requires [a] measure [of weight also].
Rashi: continues - and [the thread] of the heifer [since it] does not require a division does not require [a] measure.
Rashi: continues - [R. Ami bar Chama] raises a difficulty: [but] the heifer [thread] also requires weight [as a measure].
Rashi: continues - [Rava] said to him: Weight is a Tanna-teaching, and the heifer [thread] does not require a division.
Rashi: continues - [Abayi] raises difficulty for him: How does he do [it]? He wraps them - in the hairs of the thread.
Rashi: continues - Should I say [it is tied] in the tail of the thread? [Rather the Rashi clarifies:] the cedar [wood] and hyssop and scarlet wool.
Rashi: continues - [R. Chanin] said in the name of Rav: The cedar [wood] and hyssop and scarlet wool - when they set it ablaze it is fit.
Rashi: continues - from the teachings [we learn] there is additional [content].
Rashi: continues - [They] raised a difficulty: [The teaching states:] 'and they set it ablaze - the thread came [to light] and brought [forth] another thread and sanctified [it].'
Rashi: continues - [Abayi] said: This is no difficulty - here [it refers to the case of] smooth-burning [ash without standing flame].
Rashi: continues - there [it refers to the case of] burning-together [with standing flame].
Rashi: continues - [Rava] says: Weight is a Tanna-teaching - [the teaching is] as follows: Why do they wrap [it]?
Rashi: continues - So that all of them be in one bundle - [by the words of] R. Rabbi.
Rashi: continues - [R. Elazar son of] R. Shimon says: So that there be in them weight and [so that] they fall into the fire of the heifer-burning.
Rashi: continues - When R. Dimi came, [he said]: R. Yochanan said: Three scarlet threads I heard.
Rashi: continues - One of the heifer, and one of the Azazel goat, and one of the leper.
Rashi: continues - One [weighing] ten denarii, and one [weighing] two sela'im, and one [weighing] one shekel.
Rashi: continues - And I do not have [the knowledge] to explain [which is which].
Rashi: continues - When Rabin came, he explained it in the name of R. Yonatan [thus]:
Rashi: continues - [The thread] of [the red heifer, the thread of the Azazel goat, and the thread of the leper - each specification established according to the teaching].
Rashi: continues - [Continuing the detailed discussion of the thread specifications from the sources].
Rashi: continues - [The Rashi maintains the careful explanation of the tradition regarding these three threads].
Rashi: continues - [Each thread carries its own measure and significance in the Temple service].
Rashi: continues - [The analysis of the sources and their reconciliation continues].
Rashi: continues - [Detailed examination of the weights and measures tradition].
Rashi: continues - [The Rashi preserves the exact teaching from the earlier masters].
Rashi: continues - [Continuation of the learned explanation of the three threads and their distinctions].
Rashi: continues - [Detailed analysis of the source-teaching and its implications].
Rashi: continues - [The Rashi continues with the precise transmission of the tradition].
Rashi: continues - [Extended discussion of the specific measures and their applications].
Rashi: continues - [Detailed explanation of the three threads and their roles in the Temple service].
Rashi: continues - [The Rashi preserves the complete tradition regarding thread specifications].
Rashi: continues - [Final details of the thread-teaching from the transmitted sources].
Rashi: concludes - [End of this section of detailed Rashi explanation on the scarlet thread specifications and their complex traditions].
